Found this page: http://www.friesian.com/valley/dilemmas.htm

I like answering "moral dilemmas" because they're usually only dilemmas inasmuch as people aren't prepared to make ugly decisions and stand by them.

Here're my answers:

# 1. The Overcrowded Lifeboat

> If you had been on the jury, how would you have decided?

The people that actually threw the others overboard are guilty. If they were acting on the Captain's orders, he is guilty, too. That's a question of law, not of morals.

Morally, he chose the best choice out of a set of bad choices: If all other options are exhausted, better to be judged by 12 than carried by 6, as the saying goes.

# 2. A Father's Agonizing Choice

> What should you do?

Refuse. I will not kill my own son. Neither would I be killing the other inmate; the guard would be. Nobody can (rightfully) pin their own actions on me, and nobody can blame me for the actions of another. To do so implies that humans are not responsible for their own actions, and I do not accept that.

Also, I want to stick it to the guard and demonstrate to him and other inmates that we aren't just the guard's playthings and prevent him from receiving the reward that he was (presumably) expecting - the sick pleasure of watching a man kill his own son.

# 3. Sophie's Choice

> Did she do the right thing?

Yes - she was presented with an awful situation and there were no "right" choices, only less-bad choices. This is a case of [false implies anything](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/48161/in-classical-logic-why-is-p-rightarrow-q-true-if-both-p-and-q-are-false) - Did Sophie choose the right option of the options presented to her?

> Should she have felt guilty?

*There was no right choice and this wasn't her fault,* so while she didn't make a "right" choice, it wasn't something she could control and shouldn't feel guilty.

But she's human, so she will, regardless, and that's OK too.

# 4. Corrine's Choice

> Should Corrine Rey have been willing to sacrifice her daughter and herself rather than allow obvious murderers to enter the magazine and possibly kill everyone?

No. Not this would really be her "sacrificing" her daughter - it would be armed gunmen killing her daughter. She would not be at fault. See answer #2 - "nobody can blame me for the actions of another."

> Can a mother be blamed for only thinking of protecting her child?

No - same answer.

# 5. The Trolley Problem

> Should you flip the switch or do nothing?

If you do not flip the switch, you are a bystander in an unfortunate accident. See "Nobody can blame me for the actions of another," as described in #2 above.

If you do flip the switch, you are choosing to be a murderer (by actions that you have taken, which you must accept responsibility for) in order to reduce the total quantity of senseless loss of life that the world sees today.

Without any additional information, I would flip the switch. I would choose to live with those consequences. In a Utilitarian framework, this is morally just. In other frameworks, perhaps not.

# 6. The Fat Man and the Impeding Doom

> What should they do?

If I am not the fat man and all other options are exhausted, I use the dynamite. Better to be judged by 12 than carried by 6, as the saying goes.

# 7. The Tortured Child

> ... would you agree to do it?

No. Innocents should never be tortured, because a society that permits this admits that individual rights actually have no sanctity - and such a society *cannot* last as there is no benefit to the individuals who comprise it. At least, no society made up of human beings.

# 8. The Costly Underwater Tunnel

> What should be done?

Save the trapped worker. Presumably, each worker has signed on to the project voluntarily, and understands the risk. Every human thinks they can beat the odds; some don't. That's life and free will. To refuse to save this worker communicates that those driving the project will *intentionally* throw away the workers' lives for the success of the project. This is a very different position than undertaking a project with "expected" losses. As demonstrated by the Empire State Building's construction, we *can* do better. To refuse to save the trapped worker is to admit no interest in doing better and explicitly devalue the human lives of the workers.

> Was it a mistake to begin the tunnel in the first place?

No - assuming that the goal was to build a tunnel, and not to kill workers.

# 9. Jean Valjean's Conscience

Disclaimer: I don't know *Les Miserables*.

> Did he do the right thing?

Presuming that Jean was the mayor of the town in which the misidentified vagabond was caught, *yes* he did the right thing - as a public servant it would be wrong to allow a member of the public to suffer more than their due. In this case, Jean, a public servant, has private information which, if made public, would prevent undeserved punishment of a member of the public. It is his duty to come forward.

If he were not a public servant, but merely a private citizen, he would have no such duty to interfere in a public matter (though he would also not be wrong to come forward).

# 10. A Callous Passerby

> Does Smith have a moral obligation to save the boy?

No. He had no part in causing the situation and has no interpersonal ties to the boy. There is nothing that has any right to compel Smith to do *anything* for *anyone*, regardless of whether it's a drowning boy or a cat up a tree. Moreover, Smith has the right to blamelessly choose what he does and does not do with his life (with the usual "your rights end where another's begin" caveat).

# 11. The Last Episode of *Seinfeld*

Disclaimer: I haven't seen the episode referred to.

> They are convicted. Is this just?

The text of the "good Samaritan" law in the episode *matters.* Juries are asked to determine if a law was broken, based on the facts of a case but this question presents the situation as if we're supposed to apply our *moral* judgement to what is clearly a *legal* matter. The question is bad, and doesn't merit an answer.

However, in general, people are responsible for their own actions and nobody has any right to compel you to do something that you do not want to - so no, they were under no moral obligation to rush the robber.

# 12. A Poisonous Cup of Coffee

> Is Joe's failure to act as bad a Tom's action?

No.

The murder Tom committed (which is wrong) was premeditated and intentional. Joe's wife's death was accidental, and entirely (according to the information provided) due to her own actions.

Barring any further information about Joe and his wife and assuming no inconvenience or harm would come to Joe if he did provide the antidote, he was wrong to stand by and watch *his wife* die. This is an interpersonal relationship much different from the standard social contract by which strangers can reasonably expect interactions to be governed, and why it's not morally wrong to let the classic 'Trolley problem' trolley continue on its original course and kill the 5 strangers.

Tom intentionally put his wife's life in danger, and then stood by while she died. Joe did not put his wife's life in danger, and then stood by while she died. Tom has committed more total wrong than Joe. To be clear, they've *both* committed wrongs.

# 13. The Torture of the Mad Bomber

> ... the official thinks that it is nevertheless the right thing to do in this desperate situation. Do you agree?

No; torture of innocents is wrong. This is a repeat of #7.

# 14. The Principle of Psychiatric Confidentiality

> Should you report the threat to the police and the woman or should you remain silent as the principle of confidentiality between psychiatrist and patient demands?

Report it.

> Should there be a law that compels you to report such threats?

Yes.

A nice caveat would be that the details must remain confidential/sealed unless the *investigation* that results from the report leads to charges being filed.

15. The Partiality of Friendship

Was he right?

No.

friendship has a moral importance that permits, and perhaps even requires, partiality in some circumstances

This is incorrect.

Friendships are things that individuals desire. Individuals may prioritize friends over others in the interest of preserving or expanding the friendship and maintaining the benefits of that friendship. This is what Jim did. This is not morally defensible, but it is understandable and expected.

The paragon of virtue will have a hard time keeping friends.

That said, I also take issue with the idea of someone being "more qualified" than a "qualified" candidate. This is really just poor word choice - it would have been better to refer to the friend as "qualified" and the other candidate as "more attractive" or "a better fit for the company," since "qualified" is really just a yes/no status.

If you re-cast the question with that wording:

Should Jim give the job to his friend, who is qualified for the job, or to another candidate, who is also qualified for the job but has more to offer the company than the friend?

The answer becomes obvious!

This assumes that Jim is an ordinary employee, and not the owner of the company in question. If Jim is an employee, he's probably explicitly (via signed contract) or implicitly (via reasonable expectations based on his job position) expected to act in the best interests of the company (and surely, if he demonstrably doesn't, he'll be replaced).

If Jim is the owner, he's allowed (more or less) to run his company however he wants, and that includes prioritizing filling his staff with friends.

16. The Value of a Promise

What should you do?

Honor the promise unless/until you become legally obligated (as the laws are an extension of the social/moral contract that holds the society in which you live, together) to do otherwise, or until you no longer value the person to whom the promise was made.

In general, under what conditions should promises be broken?

Promises, unlike legal contracts, are bound by mutual respect. Once once side breaks, the promise will no longer hold.

It may well be that this person's refusal to turn themselves in eliminates the respect you held for them - in which case, by all means, turn them in!

17. The Perjured President

This is a question of law, not of morality. Why is this here? Clearly someone is miffed that Bill Clinton didn't face consequences for his blatant, self-admitted perjury to the American people's face...

Is it hypocritical of the President and his supporters to continued to support the sexual harassment and perjury laws if they do not want him to be subject to the ordinary penalties for breaking them?

Of course it's hypocritical; it couldn't be more clear-cut. "Political purposes of the President's supporters in keeping him in office" may be "more important" than following the letter of the law to some - but that's clear hypocrisy.

The President, of all people, should strictly adhere to the laws of the land and be held to the highest standards of scrutiny with the least forgiveness.
